descripcion: The past perfect has one job: to show that one past event happened before another past event. *When I arrived, he left* and *When I arrived, he had left* describe two different situations. Without it, a story told out of order becomes impossible to follow. It is a B1 structure that stays difficult through B2 because it is easy to avoid.

filas: The police arrived after the crowd **had left**.
When I got there, it **had** already **started**.
By the time we knew, it **had spread**.
"I saw it" → He said he **had seen** it.
If they **had checked**, this wouldn't have happened.

ejemplos.texto: *By the time the story was published, the company had already denied it.*
*Nobody knew the reporter had been there.*
*She said she hadn't seen the email.*
*It wasn't until the next day that we found out.*
*When I got there, it had already started.*

notas: *Before* and *after* already make the order clear, so the past perfect is optional there. With *when*, it changes the meaning, so it is not optional.
Contractions are normal and worth practising out loud: *I'd*, *he'd*, *they'd* — and *'d* is also *would*, so context decides.
English uses the past perfect more than Spanish uses the pluperfect. When in doubt about order, use it.

es.en: Spanish has the same structure (había llegado) but uses it less and often relies on context instead. Since the mechanism already exists in Spanish, this is a habit problem, not a comprehension problem.
es.es: El español tiene la misma estructura («había llegado»), pero la usa menos y a menudo confía en el contexto. Como el mecanismo ya existe en español, se trata de un problema de hábito, no de comprensión.

de.en: German has the Plusquamperfekt (war angekommen, hatte gegessen), but spoken German often replaces it with the Perfekt or Präteritum. German speakers therefore understand the English past perfect easily but under-use it in speech and in narrative.
de.de: Das Deutsche hat das Plusquamperfekt («war angekommen, hatte gegessen»), aber in der gesprochenen Sprache wird es häufig durch Perfekt oder Präteritum ersetzt. Deutschsprachige verstehen das englische past perfect daher leicht, verwenden es aber in Erzählungen und im Sprechen oft zu wenig.

it.en: Italian uses the trapassato prossimo (ero già partito quando è arrivata) quite systematically, so the English past perfect transfers well. The main difference is that Italian also uses it in some contexts where English prefers the simple past, especially in informal narrative.
it.it: L'italiano usa il trapassato prossimo («ero già partito quando è arrivata») abbastanza sistematicamente, quindi il past perfect inglese si trasferisce bene. La principale differenza è che l'italiano lo usa anche in alcuni contesti in cui l'inglese preferisce il simple past, soprattutto nel racconto informale.

fr.en: French uses the plus-que-parfait (j'étais déjà parti quand elle est arrivée) systematically, so the English past perfect transfers well. French speakers understand the sequence of events easily and mainly need to practise the English forms in fluent speech.
fr.fr: Le français utilise systématiquement le plus-que-parfait («j'étais déjà parti quand elle est arrivée»), donc le past perfect anglais se transfère bien. Les francophones comprennent facilement la chronologie et doivent surtout automatiser les formes anglaises à l'oral.

pt.en: Portuguese uses the compound pluperfect (tinha chegado) naturally in speech, and tinha + participle maps directly onto had + participle. The past perfect therefore transfers very well; the simple pluperfect (chegara) is literary and has no bearing on English.
pt.pt: O português usa naturalmente o mais-que-perfeito composto («tinha chegado») na fala, e «tinha» + particípio corresponde diretamente a «had» + particípio. O past perfect se transfere, portanto, muito bem; o mais-que-perfeito simples («chegara») é literário e não afeta o inglês.

errores: Using it for a simple sequence with no reason: *I had got up and I had had breakfast.* One past simple after another is enough.
*When I arrived he left* when you meant he was already gone.

traducciones.fr: …, ce qui n’avait pas été rapporté
traducciones.pt: …, o que não tinha sido noticiado

autochequeo: Does every past perfect mark something that really happened earlier?
Did I use it where a plain past simple would do?
Did I use it in the reported speech?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the past perfect and the order of past events. (1) Mark each past perfect and say whether it is needed. (2) Mark every place where the order is unclear and a past perfect would have fixed it. (3) Check the participles. Do not correct anything else.

es: *¡Ya te lo había dicho!* rendered as *I had told you!* instead of *I told you!*
de: Using the present perfect for the earlier past, as with the Perfekt: *When I arrived, he has already left* instead of *he had already left*.
it: *Te l'avevo detto!* rendered as *I had told you!* instead of *I told you!*
fr: *Je te l'avais dit !* rendered as *I had told you!* instead of *I told you!*
pt: *Eu tinha-te dito!* rendered as *I had told you!* instead of *I told you!*
